summary: Describes use cases and deployment scenarios for applying the Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) framework to SMTP mail. It prepares the ground for an SMTP adaptation. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Ideas for putting a helper in the mail's path that can look at or tweak each letter, and where that might be useful.

questions: email processing at the network edge
subtitle: Practical applications for processing email at network gateways using the OPES framework.

tldr.problem: Email systems need to apply policies like filtering spam, detecting viruses, and enforcing security rules, but these services are scattered and hard to coordinate across mail servers.
tldr.mechanism: OPES provides a framework where mail servers call out to external filter services via a protocol (OCP), allowing multiple independent services to inspect and modify messages in a standard way.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can deploy consistent email filtering, routing, and transformation policies by building services that work with OPES-aware mail servers.

today: RFC 4496 is Informational and documents use cases for OPES applied to SMTP. While OPES gained some adoption in research and specific deployments, many email systems evolved to handle filtering through other means, such as content scanning plugins integrated directly into mail servers.

sections.title: Introduction to OPES and Email
sections.content:
The Open Pluggable Edge Services (OPES) architecture, defined in RFC 3835, provides a general framework for intermediate services that inspect and optionally modify application-level messages. An OPES processor sits between two nodes (such as an email client and an email server) and applies services provided by external callout servers. This document applies OPES specifically to SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol), the protocol used for sending email.

In SMTP, various network intermediaries already perform filtering: mail gateways scan for viruses, mail servers check for spam, and policy engines enforce corporate rules. These services work in isolation or with proprietary integrations. The OPES framework standardizes how these services communicate with mail servers, making it easier to deploy multiple cooperating services consistently across an organization.
sections.eli5: Email goes through mail servers on the way to the recipient. OPES lets the servers ask helper programs to look at the email and do things to it, like remove viruses or mark spam, all using a standard method.

sections.title: SMTP and OPES System Architecture
sections.content:
In a typical email system, a mail client sends messages to a Mail Submission Agent (MSA) at the user's email provider. The MSA hands the message to a Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) that routes it toward the destination. Along the way, the message may pass through intermediate MTAs (gateways). Finally, a Mail Delivery Agent (MDA) at the destination stores it in the recipient's mailbox.

An OPES-aware MTA becomes an OPES processor. Instead of making filtering decisions entirely locally, it connects to external callout servers using the OCP (OPES Callout Protocol) that handle specific services: spam detection, virus scanning, policy enforcement, and so forth. The MTA sends SMTP command values and message content to the callout servers, receives responses instructing it what to do (accept, block, or modify), and then continues or rejects the mail accordingly.
sections.eli5: Email passes through a mail server. That server can ask helper computers to check the email and say 'accept it', 'block it', or 'change it' using standard commands.

sections.title: Email Service Use Cases
sections.content:
Security filtering. Callout services can examine email attachments and reject or quarantine those that contain viruses, dangerous file types, or unwanted MIME sections. The service can mark messages with warnings or add headers that downstream systems can process, and it can notify administrators of threats.

Spam filtering. Services can examine the message body and headers, compare SMTP sender and recipient addresses with the visible From/To fields (a common spam indicator), look up sender IP addresses against known spammer lists, and classify messages. Spam can be marked, moved to a spam folder, or rejected during the SMTP dialog so the sender is notified immediately.

Access control. Services can enforce policies based on sender and recipient addresses, authentication credentials, or STARTTLS status, allowing or denying mail before the message body is even examined.

Email normalization. Services can correct malformed email messages, repair unusual MIME section lengths, or detect and reject attempts to exploit vulnerabilities through malformed SMTP command values.

Secure email handling. Services can decrypt, verify signatures on, sign, or encrypt messages on behalf of the gateway, centralizing cryptographic operations. This is critical in enterprises where encryption keys are kept on secure servers rather than on end-user machines.

Message transformation. Services can re-route mail to different destinations based on policy (for example, directing employee email to the correct regional server), rewrite addresses, convert large attachments to links pointing to a web server, or perform other content-based modifications.
sections.eli5: Helpers can remove viruses, detect spam, check if the sender is allowed to send, fix broken emails, encrypt or sign them, or send them to a different place.

sections.title: Logging, Reporting, and Blocking
sections.content:
OPES services are not limited to transformation. Logging and reporting services can record details about every message without modifying it, providing audit trails and analytics for compliance. Services can access SMTP command values (sender, recipients, authentication status), message metadata (size, attachment types), or the full message body as needed.

Services can also block mail during the SMTP dialog itself. Rather than accepting a message and then filtering it later, a service can inspect the sender and recipient in the RCPT TO command and respond with an error, causing the sending server to reject the message immediately. This saves bandwidth and gives the sender immediate feedback.

These use cases cover nearly all filtering deployed at SMTP gateways today. The benefit of OPES is standardization: instead of each mail server implementing its own calling conventions for filters, OPES provides a single standard protocol that multiple vendors and service providers can implement.
sections.eli5: Services can also just watch the email and record what happened, and they can reject mail while the sender is still connected and listening.
